wrong.Bearish harami: A harami's second body sits inside the first. Day 2 opened above Day 1's close.
wrong.Shooting star: That's one candle with a long upper wick. You're looking at two candles here.

questions.simple: Dark cloud cover. Day 2 opened above Day 1's high, then closed below its middle but above its open.

deeper.trap: The midpoint is the line that matters. Find it first: halfway between Day 1's open and close. A close above it might still be a reversal, but ChartSchool would not call it a bearish dark cloud. A close below Day 1's open turns the pattern into a bearish engulfing. Day 2 here landed between the two.
deeper.counter: The sources set the open a little differently. ChartSchool asks for an open above the prior close, and Schwab for an open above the prior high. This one does both.

questions.q: A long white candle runs from a $30.00 open to a $34.00 close. Under what price does the next black candle need to close for a dark cloud?
questions.why: $32.00. The line is the middle of the white body. $30.00 plus $34.00 is $64.00, and half of that is $32.00. The black candle has to open above the $34.00 close, then close under $32.00. Close above the middle and it might still turn, but it's not a dark cloud. Work out that midpoint ahead of time, so you know what you're looking at when the candle forms.
questions.lesson_line: Find the first body's midpoint before you name a dark cloud. A close above it doesn't count.
questions.simple: Under $32.00. That's halfway between the $30.00 open and the $34.00 close.

wrong.$34.00: That's the white close. Closing there doesn't dip into the body at all.
wrong.$30.00: That's the white open. Close under it and you've got a full engulf, more than a dark cloud needs.
wrong.$31.00: That's a quarter of the way up the body. You want halfway.

questions.q: A trader says your stock just printed a harami. What did the last two candles do?
choices: A small body inside the prior big body
A big body that swallows the prior body
A whole range inside the prior range
Two candle bodies of about equal size
questions.answer: A small body inside the prior big body
questions.why: A small body tucked inside the big body before it. The first candle has a large body, and the second one's body sits inside it. Its wicks don't have to fit inside, though it's nicer when they do. Harami means pregnant in Japanese, and that's the picture: a little candle inside a big one. After a run up it hints at a turn lower. After a decline it hints at a turn higher. Either way, you're looking at the big move pausing.
questions.lesson_line: Harami is body inside body. The small second candle shows the big move paused.

wrong.A big body that swallows the prior body: That's engulfing. In a harami the second body is the small one.
wrong.A whole range inside the prior range: That's an inside day. A harami only needs the body inside the body.
wrong.Two candle bodies of about equal size: A harami needs a big first body and a small second one inside it.

questions.simple: A small body sitting inside the big body before it. The wicks don't have to fit inside.

questions.q: Your stock prints a long candle, then a doji the next day that sits inside that long body. What's the pattern called?
questions.why: Harami cross. It's a harami where the second candle is a doji, and that doji sits fully inside the long candle's real body. So you get a big move, then a session where nobody won. If the doji gapped away from that body instead, it'd be in star position, and you'd call it a doji star. Same doji, different spot, different name. I read it like any harami: the move paused, and the next candle picks the side.
questions.lesson_line: A doji inside a long body is a harami cross. A doji that gaps away is a doji star.

wrong.Morning doji star: In a doji star the doji gaps away from the first candle. Here it sits inside the first body.
wrong.Bullish engulfing: Engulfing needs a big second body covering the first. A doji has almost no body.
wrong.Spinning top: A spinning top is one candle with a small body and long wicks. You've got two candles here, and the second is a doji.

questions.simple: A harami cross. The second candle is a doji that sits inside the first candle's body.

questions.story: Your stock has rallied for two weeks. Day 1 is a long white candle from $40.00 to $44.00. Day 2 opens at $43.20 and closes at $42.80.
questions.q: What did those two days just print?
questions.why: Bearish harami. Day 2's small body, $43.20 down to $42.80, sits inside Day 1's long white body from $40.00 to $44.00. It came after a two-week rally, so you call it the bearish kind. That's the big move pausing. Don't treat it as a sell signal yet. Watch which way the next candles break. After a decline, the same pattern reads as a possible turn higher.
questions.lesson_line: Body inside body makes a harami. The trend before it says which kind.

wrong.Bearish engulfing: Engulfing needs the second body to swallow the first. Day 2's body is the smaller one.
wrong.Dark cloud cover: A dark cloud opens above Day 1's close. Day 2 opened at $43.20, below Day 1's $44.00 close.
wrong.Evening star: An evening star takes three candles, and its small middle one gaps above the first body. Day 2 opened at $43.20, inside Day 1's body, and there's no third day.

questions.simple: Bearish harami. Day 2's small body sits inside Day 1's long white body, right after a rally.

questions.q: After a rally, your stock prints a bearish harami. That tells you it's about to turn down.
questions.why: False. A harami after a run up is a possible turn, not a sure one. The small second candle just says the move paused. Plenty of them break either way. So I read it as a pause and wait. If it breaks lower, now you've got your answer. If it breaks higher, the run is back on, and you didn't sell a good stock on a guess.
questions.lesson_line: A harami is a pause. The break that follows tells you which way.
questions.simple: False. A bearish harami only hints at a turn, and the next candles have to confirm it.

deeper.trap: The name sounds like a forecast. Bearish harami tells you where it formed, after an advance, not what comes next. Fidelity's slides say that although common belief is that the harami is a reversal pattern, many report it can break either way. Treat it as a pause and let the break pick the side.

questions.q: Inside days come up all the time on our charts. What does a stock have to do to print one?
choices: High and low inside the prior range
Body inside the prior day's body
Smaller range than the prior day
Open and close about the same price
questions.answer: High and low inside the prior range
questions.why: Its high and low both stay inside yesterday's range. The whole day, wicks included, fits within the day before. That's the range tightening and volatility easing off. Don't mix it up with a harami, which only needs the body inside the body. In a good setup I like seeing them, because tight is where you find a clean entry. A push over the inside day's high can be your trigger.
questions.lesson_line: Inside day is range inside range. It's the stock getting tight.

wrong.Body inside the prior day's body: That's a harami. An inside day looks at the high and the low, not just the body.
wrong.Smaller range than the prior day: Not enough on its own. The high and the low both have to stay inside yesterday's range.

questions.simple: Its high and low both stay inside yesterday's range. It shows the stock getting tight.

questions.story: Monday: open $49.00, high $52.00, low $48.00, close $49.40. Tuesday: open $50.50, high $51.20, low $48.90, close $50.80.
questions.q: How would you label Tuesday?
questions.why: Inside day. Tuesday's range, $48.90 to $51.20, sits completely inside Monday's $48.00 to $52.00. But you can't call it a harami. Tuesday's body, $50.50 to $50.80, sits above Monday's $49.00 to $49.40 body, not inside it. An inside day tests the range. A harami tests the body. Tuesday's high and low are now your levels to watch for the break.
questions.lesson_line: Check the range for an inside day and the body for a harami. They're different tests.

wrong.Harami: A harami's body sits inside the prior body. Tuesday's body, $50.50 to $50.80, is above Monday's $49.00 to $49.40 body.
wrong.Outside day: An outside day breaks both the prior high and the prior low. Tuesday did neither.
wrong.Bullish engulfing: Engulfing needs Tuesday's body to cover Monday's. The two bodies don't even overlap.

questions.simple: Inside day. Its high and low stay within Monday's range, but its body sits above Monday's body.

deeper.trap: The two tests can split. A day can sit inside the prior range while its body sits outside the prior body, as here. It can also go the other way: a small body inside the prior body, with a high above the prior high. That is a harami but not an inside day, since a harami's shadows need not fit inside.

questions.q: Today is an inside day on your stock. The candle itself tells you which way it'll break.
questions.why: False. An inside day tells you the range got tighter. It doesn't tell you the direction. So you plan both sides, and the inside day's high and low become your lines. In a healthy uptrend, the push over the high is the one I care about. A break under the low tells you to wait.
questions.lesson_line: An inside day gives you levels, not direction. Its high and low are the lines to watch.
questions.simple: False. An inside day only shows the range getting tight, not which way the stock breaks.

deeper.trap: A tight day can feel like a hint about direction. It is not a forecast. Investopedia says a series of inside days may signal a coming reversal. Yet the breakout direction can't be predicted from the pattern alone. Plan for both sides and let price choose.
deeper.example: Fidelity's inside-bar plan trades both ways. It buys the next bar on an open above the inside bar's close, and sells on an open below it.

questions.q: Someone calls today an outside day on your stock. What did it have to do?
choices: Higher high and lower low than prior
High and low both inside the prior range
Body swallows the prior day's body
Gaps above the prior day's high
questions.answer: Higher high and lower low than prior
questions.why: Higher high and lower low than the day before. The whole range covers yesterday's range, at both ends. Don't mix it up with engulfing, which only needs the body to cover the prior body. An outside day needs the high and the low. That's a wide day, the opposite of tight. Then look at the close, because that tells you who won the fight. After a run, an outside day that closes down near the low is one I respect.
questions.lesson_line: Outside day: range covers range, at both ends.

wrong.Body swallows the prior day's body: That's engulfing, which only needs the bodies. An outside day needs the whole range.
wrong.Gaps above the prior day's high: A gap up only says where it opened. An outside day has to trade above the prior high and below the prior low.
wrong.High and low both inside the prior range: That's an inside day, the opposite.

questions.simple: It trades above yesterday's high and below yesterday's low, so its range covers the whole day before.

questions.story: Your stock has rallied for three weeks. Today it trades above yesterday's high, then falls below yesterday's low. It closes down near the low.
questions.q: What's the name for a day like that?
questions.why: Outside reversal day. It's an outside day, with a high over yesterday's high and a low under yesterday's low. And it closed against the trend. After three weeks up, that means a down close. Buyers took out yesterday's high and then got overrun. That's a possible trend change, not a sure one. Volume and the level it hits add weight, so you check both.
questions.lesson_line: An outside day that closes against the trend is an outside reversal. Volume and the level it hits add weight.

wrong.Inside day pattern: An inside day stays within yesterday's range. Today broke out of both ends.
wrong.Harami cross: A harami cross needs a doji tucked inside the prior body. Today's range swallowed yesterday's.
wrong.Morning star: A morning star is a three-candle turn after a decline. This is one day, after a rally.

questions.simple: An outside reversal day. It broke both ends of yesterday's range and closed down against the rally.

deeper.trap: Don't mix it up with bearish engulfing. Engulfing only needs today's body to cover yesterday's body. ChartSchool says the outside reversal needs the entire range engulfed, high and low, not just the open and close. So a day can be one without being the other. Check the shadows, then the close against the trend.

questions.q: Morning and evening stars get their name from one candle in the middle. When is a candle in star position?
choices: Its small body gaps from the prior body
It opens at the prior candle's close
It has no shadow above or below its body
It closes right at the session's high
questions.answer: Its small body gaps from the prior body
questions.why: When its small body gaps away from the candle before it. It stands off on its own, apart from everything before it. The gap can be up or down. The star itself has a small body, so a doji, a hammer, a shooting star or a spinning top can all sit there. It's the gap that makes it a star, not the wicks or where it closes. After a long run or a long slide I mark it, then let the next candle tell me if the move is turning.
questions.lesson_line: A star is a small body standing apart after a gap. It's the middle of the morning and evening star.

wrong.It opens at the prior candle's close: Then there's no gap. A star gaps away from the candle before it.
wrong.It has no shadow above or below its body: That's a marubozu. A star is about the gap, not the wicks.
wrong.It closes right at the session's high: Where it closes in its own range doesn't make a star. The gap does.

questions.simple: When its small body gaps away from the candle before it and stands off on its own.

questions.q: After a slide, a long black candle, then a small one that gaps lower. Then a long white one closes past the black's middle. Name it.
questions.why: Morning star. Three candles, at the end of a downtrend. First a long black candle. Then a small one that gaps below the black close, where the selling stalls out. Then a long white candle that closes above the middle of the first body. That third candle is your confirmation, the one that does the work. If the middle one is a doji, you've got a morning doji star.
questions.lesson_line: Morning star: down, pause, up. The third candle is the one that does the work.

wrong.Evening star: That's the bearish mirror, and it forms after a run up. Here the first candle is black.
wrong.Three white soldiers: That's three long white candles in a row. The first candle here is black.
wrong.Bullish harami: A harami is two candles, with the second inside the first. This takes three, and the middle one gaps away.

questions.simple: Morning star. A long black candle, a small one that gaps lower, then a long white candle.

questions.q: Your stock has been running for weeks. Which three-candle sequence would make an evening star?
choices: Up candle, small gap-up, down candle
Down candle, small gap-down, up candle
Three long down candles in a row
Up candle, then a doji inside it
questions.answer: Up candle, small gap-up, down candle
questions.why: Up candle, small gap-up, down candle. First a big white candle. Then a small one that gaps above that body. That's the run stalling out. Then a down candle finishes it. You're looking at the mirror of the morning star, which shows up after a decline. Three black candles in a row would be three black crows instead.
questions.lesson_line: Evening star: up, pause, down. The small middle candle is the pause.

wrong.Down candle, small gap-down, up candle: That's the morning star, the mirror image after a decline.
wrong.Up candle, then a doji inside it: That's a harami cross. A star's middle candle gaps away from the first.

questions.simple: A big up candle, then a small one that gaps above it, then a down candle.

questions.q: In a morning star, the small middle candle can be either white or black.
questions.why: True. ChartSchool describes the middle candle as a small white or black candle that gaps below the prior close. Investopedia agrees it can be black or white. What makes it a star is the small body and the gap down. If it is a doji, the pattern is called a morning doji star.
questions.lesson_line: In a star pattern, the middle candle's size and gap matter. Its color doesn't.
questions.simple: True, because the middle candle's small body and its gap matter, not its color.

questions.story: Day 1 on your stock is a long black candle from $50.00 down to $45.00. Day 2 gaps lower and opens and closes at $44.20. Day 3 opens at $45.20 and closes at $48.50.
questions.q: What do those three days add up to?
questions.why: Morning doji star. Day 1 is a long black candle, $50.00 down to $45.00. Day 2 gaps under that and opens and closes at $44.20. That's a doji sitting in star position. Day 3 is a long white candle that closes at $48.50, well above the middle of Day 1's body. So you've got a morning star whose middle candle is a doji. Sellers ran out, and buyers took over.
questions.lesson_line: When the small middle candle is a doji, the morning star becomes a morning doji star.

wrong.Evening doji star: That's the top version: long white, doji, long black.
wrong.Harami cross: In a harami cross the doji sits inside the first body. Here the doji gapped below it.
wrong.Three white soldiers: That needs three long white candles. Day 1 is black and Day 2 is a doji.

questions.simple: Morning doji star. A doji gaps below a long black candle, then a long white candle follows.

deeper.trap: Check where the doji sits. Below the first body, after a gap, it is in star position, so this is a morning doji star. Inside the first body, the same doji would make a harami cross. The doji looks the same in both. Its position names the pattern.

questions.q: A trader says your stock just put in three white soldiers. What did it do?
choices: Three long white candles in a row
Three small candles in a big one
Three long black ones in a row
questions.answer: Three long white candles in a row
questions.why: Three long white candles in a row. Each one opens inside the body before it, closes near its high and closes over the prior day's high. So they don't gap up at the open. They just march higher, day after day. That's buyers stepping in every single session. Flip it to three long black candles and you've got three black crows.
questions.lesson_line: Soldiers march up, crows fly down. Both are three long bodies in a row.

wrong.Three small candles in a big one: That's the middle of a rising three methods.
wrong.Three white candles gapping up: Each soldier opens inside the body before it, not above it. Gaps at the open break the pattern.

questions.simple: Three long white candles in a row, each one opening inside the body before it and closing near its high.

deeper.example: ChartSchool says each soldier should open within the previous body and close near the high of the day. Investopedia adds that each close exceeds the previous candle's high.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Three long black candles in a row, each closing near its low, are called ___.
questions.why: Three black crows. ChartSchool describes three long black bodies in a row. Each opens within the prior body and closes at or near its low. Schwab adds that they close progressively lower. Three white soldiers is the up version. As a bearish reversal pattern, it needs an uptrend before it.
questions.lesson_line: Three black crows show sellers in charge three sessions running.
questions.simple: Three black crows, because three long black candles in a row, each closing near its low, show sellers in charge.

questions.q: Your stock prints a long white candle, rests three days inside its range, then closes at a new high. What's that pattern?
questions.why: Rising three methods. The long white candle comes first. Then three small candles stay inside its high and low. That's the stock resting, not turning. Then a fifth candle closes at a new high. It's a continuation pattern. The trend took a short break and kept going. Tight little rest, then the push. That's the kind of action I like to see.
questions.lesson_line: Rising three methods is a rest inside a big up candle, then a push to a new high.

wrong.Three white soldiers: That's three long white candles back to back, with no small ones resting in between.
wrong.Bullish harami: A harami is two candles. This pattern takes five.
wrong.Morning star: A morning star starts with a long black candle after a decline. This starts with a long white one.

questions.simple: Rising three methods. Small candles rest inside a long white candle's range, then it pushes to a new high.

questions.q: You wait for a candle pattern to trigger, a break in one direction, before you act on it.
questions.why: True. A pattern is a question, and the break is the answer. A bullish pattern needs more upside after it. That can be a gap up, a long white candle or an advance on heavy volume. Most patterns need that confirmation. Buy before it and you're guessing. I'd rather pay a little more and know it's working.
questions.lesson_line: A candle pattern asks a question. The next candle answers it.
questions.simple: True. A pattern is only a hint until price breaks one way and backs it up.

reasons: fixed before (checker corrected the Schwab sentence)

deeper.example: Fidelity warns not to act on a perceived candle pattern until it has formed and a breakout in one direction activates it. ChartSchool says most reversal patterns need confirmation.

questions.story: After a two-week slide, your stock prints a bullish engulfing. The next day it gaps down and closes below the engulfing candle's low.
questions.q: What's your read on the pattern now?
choices: Confirmed: a gap down is a dip to buy
Unconfirmed, but buy: the shape is good
questions.why: Unconfirmed. The next day disagreed. Confirmation would have been more upside: a gap up, a long white candle, a move over the engulfing candle's high. That move over the high is the trigger I'd want. Instead it gapped down and closed under the engulfing candle's low. The shape was textbook, and it doesn't matter. The market said no, so you don't argue with it.
questions.lesson_line: The pattern asked a question and the next day said no. I'd rather wait than argue with it.

wrong.Confirmed: the shape was textbook: Shape never confirms. You need more strength after the pattern.
wrong.Confirmed: a gap down is a dip to buy: A gap down is the opposite of follow-through. It closed under the pattern's low.
wrong.Unconfirmed, but buy: the shape is good: Buying a pattern that just failed is hoping, not trading. The break went down, not up.

questions.simple: Unconfirmed. The next day gapped down and closed under the pattern's low instead of moving higher.

deeper.trap: A perfect shape tempts you to buy anyway. But the shape only asks a question. ChartSchool wants further strength to confirm a bullish reversal. Investopedia names a move above the engulfing candle's high as the trigger. A close below its low is the opposite answer.

questions.q: Your stock prints a bullish engulfing right at a new high. That's still a bullish reversal.
questions.why: False. There's nothing to reverse. A bullish reversal needs a downtrend before it. At a new high, an engulfing candle just shows buyers are still pushing. That's closer to a continuation. And it's not bad news. It's a strong stock acting strong. Just don't call it a bottom.
questions.lesson_line: Check the trend before you name the pattern. No downtrend, no bullish reversal.
questions.simple: False. A reversal needs a downtrend to turn, and at a new high there isn't one.

deeper.counter: Same shape, two meanings. After a two-week slide, a bullish engulfing is a possible reversal that still needs confirmation. At a new high, ChartSchool reads it as continued buying, closer to a continuation pattern. Name the trend first, then the pattern.

reasons: key rests on one publisher (ChartSchool f71, f16, f70); Investopedia f136 supports only the bearish mirror

questions.story: Yesterday your stock closed at $50.00. Today it gaps up, opens at $53.00, drifts lower and closes at $52.00.
questions.q: Is today's candle hollow or filled?
choices: Filled: it closed below its open
Neither: it's a doji, a thin line
Hollow: buyers gapped it up at the open
questions.answer: Filled: it closed below its open
questions.why: Filled. The fill compares today's $52.00 close with today's $53.00 open. Yesterday's $50.00 close doesn't come into it. Closing below the open draws a filled candle, with the open at the top of the body. So your stock is up on the day and still prints a filled candle. It gapped up and faded all session. That fade is worth noticing.
questions.lesson_line: A filled candle can still be up on the day. The fill compares the close with its own open.

wrong.Hollow: it's up from yesterday: The day's change doesn't decide the fill. A close below the open makes it filled.
wrong.Neither: it's a doji, a thin line: A doji needs the open and close about equal. $53.00 down to $52.00 is a real body.
wrong.Hollow: buyers gapped it up at the open: The gap sets where it opened, not the fill. The $52.00 close under the $53.00 open makes it filled.

questions.simple: Filled. The $52.00 close is under the $53.00 open, even though the stock is up on the day.

questions.q: Switch your chart from candles to bars, and you see the same four prices for each day.
questions.why: True. Both show the open, high, low and close. A bar marks them with little lines. A candle draws the open-to-close part as a colored body. Same data, different picture. I use candles because the body makes the open and the close jump out at you. A line chart is the one that drops data and only connects the closes.
questions.lesson_line: Bars and candles hold the same data. Candles make the open-close story easier to see.
questions.simple: True. Bars and candles both show the open, high, low and close, just drawn differently.

questions.story: Your stock opens at $30.00 and sells off to $27.50 by midday. By the close it's back at $30.40, near the high.
questions.q: What's that long lower wick telling you?
choices: Buyers took back a deep drop
Heavy volume came in at the low
questions.answer: Buyers took back a deep drop
questions.why: Buyers took back a deep drop. Sellers drove it down to $27.50 during the day. Then buyers bid it all the way back to close at $30.40, above the $30.00 open. That's demand showing up. It tells you what happened today, not what happens tomorrow. Don't treat that $27.50 low as your stop on a buy near $30.40 though. It's far too wide for me. I'd want the next candle to push over today's high, or a tighter spot, before I get involved.
questions.lesson_line: A long lower wick shows where buyers showed up. It describes today, it doesn't promise tomorrow.

wrong.Sellers controlled the close: The close was near the high. A small body up top means buyers took over by the end.
wrong.It will go higher tomorrow: A candle describes one session. Wait for the next one to break higher before you act.
wrong.Heavy volume came in at the low: A candle only holds the open, high, low and close. Check the volume bars for volume.

questions.simple: Buyers took back a deep drop. Sellers pushed it to $27.50, but it closed above the open.

questions.story: Your stock at new highs spikes 6% in the first hour. By the close it has given almost all of it back and finishes near its open.
questions.q: What's the long upper wick telling you?
choices: Buyers won: it made a new high
Sellers will push it lower tomorrow
questions.why: Sellers pushed back the rally. Buyers ran it to a new high early. By the close, sellers had dragged it back near the open. The breakout didn't hold today. That's a yellow flag, not a red one, and it doesn't tell you what happens tomorrow. Mark the high it got rejected from. If the next candle breaks lower, that's your confirmation. If it pushes back through the high, the wick didn't mean much.
questions.lesson_line: A long upper wick is a rally that didn't hold. The close tells you who won the day.

wrong.Buyers held the day's gains: They didn't. It finished near the open after spiking 6%.
wrong.Buyers won: it made a new high: It touched a new high but couldn't hold it. The close near the open says sellers won the back half.
wrong.Sellers will push it lower tomorrow: One candle describes one session. Wait for the next candle before you call it.

questions.simple: Sellers pushed back the rally. It spiked early but gave almost all of it back by the close.

deeper.trap: At a new high, a long upper shadow feels like the top. It might not be. Schwab says signs that a rally may be ending usually amount to yellow flags, not red ones. ChartSchool says most bearish patterns require bearish confirmation. Note the high it rejected and watch what the next candle does.

questions.q: Today's candle: open $40.00, high $41.50, low $39.60, close $41.20. How big is the real body?
questions.why: $1.20. The body runs from the open to the close. $41.20 minus $40.00 is $1.20. The $41.50 high and the $39.60 low are the wicks, so they stay out of it. It closed above the open, so the body is hollow. Make this one automatic, because everything else on a candle gets measured against the body.
questions.lesson_line: Body is close minus open. Leave the high and the low out of it.
questions.simple: $1.20. The body runs from the $40.00 open to the $41.20 close, and the wicks don't count.

wrong.$1.90: That's high minus low, the whole range, wicks included.
wrong.$1.50: You went from the open to the high, so you added the upper wick.
wrong.$1.60: You went from the low to the close, so you added the lower wick.

questions.q: Open $25.00, high $27.40, low $24.80, close $25.30 on your stock. How long is the upper wick?
questions.why: $2.10. First find the top of the body. The $25.30 close is above the $25.00 open, so the close is the top. The upper wick runs from there to the $27.40 high. $27.40 minus $25.30 is $2.10. Measuring from the open is the common slip. On a hollow candle the open is the bottom of the body.
questions.lesson_line: Upper wick is the high minus the top of the body. On a hollow candle, the top is the close.
questions.simple: $2.10. The upper wick runs from the $25.30 close at the top of the body to the $27.40 high.

wrong.$2.40: You measured from the open. On a hollow candle that's the bottom of the body.
wrong.$2.60: That's high minus low, the whole range.
wrong.$2.30: You tacked on the lower wick. It isn't part of the upper one.

questions.q: Here's the candle: open $60.00, high $60.10, low $57.00, close $59.40. How long is the lower wick?
questions.why: $2.40. This one closed under its open, $59.40 against $60.00, so it's a filled candle. On a filled candle the close is the bottom of the body. The lower wick runs from $59.40 down to the $57.00 low. $59.40 minus $57.00 is $2.40. Measure from the open and you'd be counting the body as wick.
questions.lesson_line: On a filled candle the bottom of the body is the close. Measure the lower wick from there.
questions.simple: $2.40. On this filled candle the bottom of the body is the $59.40 close, so measure down from there.

deeper.trap: One easy slip is to measure every lower shadow from the open. That works only on a hollow candle, where the open is the bottom of the body. On a filled candle the close is the bottom, so start there. From the $60.00 open you would be adding the whole body to the shadow.

wrong.$0.70: You measured from the close up to the high. That's not the lower wick.
wrong.$0.10: That's the upper wick, the high minus the open.

questions.story: Your stock has slid for a month. Today it opens at $22.00, rallies to $24.10, and fades to close at $22.50. The low is $21.90.
questions.q: What's the right name for today's candle?
questions.why: Inverted hammer. The body is small and near the bottom, $22.00 to $22.50. The upper wick runs all the way to $24.10, and the lower wick is tiny. It came after a month of sliding. After a rally, the same shape would be a shooting star. There's a real body, so it's no gravestone doji. Buyers tried and couldn't hold it, so you still need a strong next candle before you act.
questions.lesson_line: After a decline, a long upper wick shows buyers tried. They still need the next candle to prove it.

wrong.Shooting star: Same shape, but a shooting star forms after a run up. This one came after a month-long slide.
wrong.Hammer: A hammer's long wick is below the body. This one's is on top.
wrong.Gravestone doji: A gravestone has the open, low and close together, with no real body. This one closed at $22.50 against a $22.00 open.

questions.simple: Inverted hammer. A long upper wick and a small body near the low, after a long slide.

deeper.trap: The long upper shadow looks bearish, so it is easy to call it a shooting star. The trend decides the name. After a decline it is an inverted hammer. But it still shows a rally that failed by the close. So ChartSchool says bullish confirmation is required before action.

conflicts: Hammer vs hanging man: ChartSchool (Introduction to Candlesticks) and Investopedia (Hanging Man) say the two look identical and are named by the trend before them; the body can be black or white. Fidelity's webinar slides (citing Kirkpatrick and Dahlquist) say they are 'differentiated by the color of the body' and that hammers have white bodies and shooting stars black ones. The unit follows ChartSchool and Investopedia (q22, q27, w2) and asks no question about the color of a hammer, hanging man, inverted hammer or shooting star.

Harami colors: ChartSchool's Pattern Dictionary and Glossary H, and Investopedia's Candlestick page, say the second candle is the opposite color. ChartSchool's reversal-pattern pages (citing Nison's Beyond Candlesticks) and Fidelity's slides say any color combination counts. No question asks a harami's colors (q33, q35, q38 rest only on body inside body).

Engulfing and the shadows: ChartSchool (Dictionary, bullish and bearish pages), Investopedia's Bullish Engulfing page and Fidelity's slides judge engulfing on the bodies only. Investopedia's Bearish Engulfing page says the body is what matters 'not the changes in the wicks', but its next takeaway also says 'the high must be higher and the low must be lower'. q28, q29 and q30 key the body-only definition the sources share; q29 asks whether every engulfing is an outside day (False), which holds under the majority definition. Checker, 2026-11-09: Investopedia's Bullish Engulfing page has the same split: it says the body is judged 'without regard to the length of the tail shadows', then describes the second day opening 'lower than the previous low' and closing 'higher than the previous high'. ChartSchool states outright that engulfing 'does not require the entire range (high and low) to be engulfed', so q29 stands.

Doji strictness: Fidelity's slides say a doji's open and close are 'the same price'. ChartSchool ('virtually equal', 'Ideally, but not necessarily') and Investopedia ('the same or very close to it'; dragonfly page: 'slight discrepancies') allow a small difference. q10 keys the looser rule, held by two publishers.

Candle color: ChartSchool, Investopedia (Real Body), CME and Schwab say the color compares the close with the same candle's open; CME adds 'depending on the color settings of your software' and Fidelity says 'most commonly'. Investopedia's Candlestick page (Bottom Line) says the color shows the close against 'the previous period'. Checker, 2026-11-09: StockCharts' own SharpCharts FAQ (s36) says its default draws a candle black or red by the prior day's close and hollow or filled by the open, so a gap up that fades but closes above the prior close is a filled black candle there. The fill rule is the same everywhere: q53 now keys the fill only (it said 'Filled (red)'), q15 asks the convention ('most charting platforms') and names the StockCharts exception, and w1 says 'most charts'.

Dark cloud cover open: ChartSchool says the black candle opens above the previous close; Schwab says above the previous high; Investopedia lists a gap up. q31's story opens above both the prior close and the prior high, so it qualifies under all three; q32 asks only for the midpoint, which all three agree on.

Shooting star gap: ChartSchool reports Greg Morris wants a gap up while Nison shows one without, and concludes 'the essence of the reversal should not be lost without the gap'. q24's story does not mention a gap and its key does not rest on one.

Star: Investopedia's Star page describes the small body appearing 'above the prior candle's range' (the evening-star case). ChartSchool says a star gaps up or down. q42 keys 'gaps away', which covers both, and cites both pages.

Bar vs candle: Schwab says the candlestick chart 'offers traders more information' than a bar chart. CME ('a bar chart provides four pieces of data ... the open, high, low and close'; 'Candlestick charts take the same information as a bar chart') and Fidelity agree the two carry the same four prices; Schwab's 'more' reads as the visual body and color. q54 keys the same-four-prices fact.

Three white soldiers: ChartSchool says each close should be near the high of the day; Investopedia says each close exceeds the previous candle's high. q47 keys only what both say: three long white candles in a row, each opening inside the prior body.

Marubozu: ChartSchool's Introduction and Investopedia define the full marubozu, with no upper or lower shadow. ChartSchool's Pattern Dictionary also counts a candle with no shadow at only one end (the open or the close). q19, q20 and q21 use the full version, which both publishers share.

Sources left out on purpose: Thomas Bulkowski's ThePatternSite.com states the site 'shall not be used to train artificial intelligence (AI) systems', and docs/study/TRAINING_CORPUS.md makes the whole Study module training material for UCT's own analysis system. To stay clear of that notice this unit cites no thepatternsite.com page; every key stands on ChartSchool, Investopedia, Schwab, Fidelity and CME. The owner may decide whether Bulkowski can be cited.
